sections.title: Object Becomes Possessor
sections.content: When a transitive verb phrase like 'átfogalmazza a szöveget' (he rephrases the text) is nominalized with -ás/-és, the former direct object loses its -t accusative suffix and becomes the POSSESSOR, while the -ás/-és noun takes the 3rd-person possessive suffix (-a/-e/-ja/-je): 'a szöveg átfogalmazása' (the rephrasing of the text), 'a kérdés megválaszolása' (the answering of the question).

sections.title: Double Possessive Chains with -nak/-nek
sections.content: When that nominalization itself possesses another abstract noun (such as 'titka', 'fontossága', 'célja'), the first nominalization takes the dative possessor ending -nak/-nek: 'a kötet sikerének a titka' (the secret of the volume's success), 'a szöveg átfogalmazásának a célja' (the goal of the rephrasing of the text).

items.spanish: A kötet átütő sikerének a titka a pontos megfigyelésben rejlett.
items.english: The secret of the volume's breakthrough success lay in accurate observation.

items.english: The imitation of Babits's complex periodic sentences succeeded masterfully.

sections.title: B2 Stylistic Notice
sections.content: In a double possessive chain, always put -nak/-nek on the middle link ('a kötet sikerének a titka') so the reader knows where the first possession ends and the main head noun begins.
